title: Syncope
subject: Medicine
summary: Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness due to cerebral hypoperfusion. Identify precipitating factors, assess severity, and rule out life‑threatening causes quickly, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Syncope is a sudden, brief loss of consciousness with spontaneous recovery, caused by a temporary drop in cerebral blood flow.
b: Diagnose by history of rapid onset, short duration (<1 min), and full recovery.
Exclude seizures (post‑ictal confusion) and metabolic encephalopathy.

sections.p: Use the ESC/ACC risk stratification: high‑risk (cardiac cause, structural heart disease, exertional syncope), intermediate, and low‑risk (vasovagal, orthostatic).
b: High‑risk features: chest pain, exertional syncope, heart disease, abnormal ECG, trauma.
Low‑risk: clear trigger, prodrome, normal exam, no cardiac history.

sections.p: Classify by mechanism: cardiac, reflex (neurally mediated), orthostatic, and miscellaneous.
b: Cardiac: aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, acute MI, tamponade.
Reflex: vasovagal, carotid sinus hypersensitivity, situational (cough, micturition).
Orthostatic: dehydration, autonomic failure, medication (diuretics, antihypertensives).
Miscellaneous: anemia, severe infection (malaria, TB sepsis), pulmonary embolism, sickle‑cell crisis.

sections.p: Patients report a prodrome (light‑headedness, nausea, sweating) followed by a brief loss of consciousness and rapid recovery.
b: Prodrome present in reflex syncope; absent in cardiac arrhythmia.
Exertional syncope suggests fixed outflow obstruction (aortic stenosis) or severe pulmonary hypertension.

t.b: Detect arrhythmia, ischemia, conduction block; abnormal findings raise cardiac risk.
Answers if drop >20 mmHg systolic or >10 mmHg diastolic on standing; positive suggests orthostatic cause.
Assesses valve disease, LV function, pericardial effusion; absence of equipment → refer or use bedside cardiac exam.
Identify anemia, electrolyte imbalance, hypoglycaemia; treat if abnormal.
Looks for pulmonary infiltrates, cardiomegaly, signs of PE; if unavailable, focus on clinical PE clues.

sections.p: Immediate danger arises from cardiac causes, massive PE, aortic stenosis, or severe dehydration.
b: Syncope with chest pain, dyspnoea, or palpitations.
Traumatic injury from fall.
Persistent hypotension after the event.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, ensure safety, and monitor for recurrence.
b: Cardiac: urgent cardiology referral, consider anti‑arrhythmic or valve replacement; avoid β‑blockers in severe aortic stenosis without specialist input.
Reflex: education, physical counter‑pressure maneuvers, avoid triggers; midodrine if severe orthostatic intolerance.
Orthostatic: fluid repletion, review diuretics/antihypertensives, compression stockings.
Infection‑related: treat malaria, TB, or sepsis promptly; correct anemia.

sections.p: Arrange review within 1 week for high‑risk patients; low‑risk can be outpatient after discharge.
b: Educate on trigger avoidance, hydration, and when to call emergency services.
Repeat ECG and orthostatic vitals at follow‑up.

sections.p: Distinguish syncope from seizures, transient ischemic attack, and metabolic encephalopathy.
b: Seizure: post‑ictal confusion, tongue biting, urinary incontinence.
TIA: focal neurological deficit lasting >5 min, no rapid recovery.
Hypoglycaemia: low glucose with neuroglycopenic symptoms, treat with glucose.

sections.p: Normal ECG does not exclude cardiac syncope; orthostatic vitals can be falsely normal if patient is supine too long.
b: Intermittent arrhythmias may need Holter or event monitor.
Mild anemia may still cause syncope in severe malaria.

whenToSeekHelp: Syncope with chest pain, palpitations, or dyspnoea
Persistent low blood pressure or altered mental state after the event

faq.q: Why does exertional syncope suggest aortic stenosis?
faq.a: Exercise raises demand; a fixed valve cannot increase output, causing cerebral hypoperfusion.

faq.q: Can a normal ECG rule out a cardiac cause?
faq.a: No; intermittent arrhythmias or structural disease may be missed without further testing.

faq.q: What bedside maneuver helps a vasovagal episode?
faq.a: Leg crossing and muscle tensing increase venous return and prevent fainting.

exam: What immediate investigations are mandatory in a patient with syncope on exertion? — ECG, orthostatic BP, focused cardiac exam, and bedside ultrasound if possible; they identify cardiac obstruction or arrhythmia.
How would you differentiate vasovagal syncope from a cardiac arrhythmia at the bedside? — Look for prodrome, trigger, and examine pulse; absence of prodrome and irregular pulse point to arrhythmia.
A 55‑year‑old with known aortic stenosis faints while climbing stairs. What is the next step? — Treat as high‑risk cardiac syncope; arrange urgent cardiology review for possible valve replacement.

Why is midodrine preferred over fludrocortisone for chronic orthostatic syncope in low‑resource settings? — Midodrine works quickly without causing fluid overload, which is safer where monitoring is limited.
What red‑flag symptom would make you suspect pulmonary embolism in a syncope patient? — Sudden dyspnoea with pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and hypotension.

Explain why a patient on antihypertensives may develop orthostatic syncope after a diarrhoeal illness. — Volume loss plus medication‑induced vasodilation reduces standing BP, leading to cerebral hypoperfusion.
How does sickle‑cell crisis precipitate syncope? — Severe anaemia and vaso‑occlusion reduce oxygen delivery, causing cerebral hypoperfusion.
What is the role of compression stockings in syncope management? — They improve venous return, reducing orthostatic drops in blood pressure.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Collect a focused history and perform a systematic exam to differentiate cardiac, reflex, orthostatic and miscellaneous causes of syncope.
b: History: onset (sudden vs gradual), duration (<1 min), prodrome (light‑headedness, nausea, diaphoresis), trigger (position, exertion, cough, micturition), recovery (complete, residual confusion), precipitating events (medication change, dehydration), family history of sudden death, comorbidities (heart disease, diabetes, HIV).
Exam: vital signs supine and standing (measure BP/HR at 1 min and 3 min), look for orthostatic drop (≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic).

Cardiac auscultation: harsh systolic murmur radiating to carotids (aortic stenosis), crescendo‑decrescendo murmur increasing with Valsalva (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), diastolic rumble (mitral stenosis).
Neurologic: check for post‑ictal confusion, focal deficits, seizure‑like activity.
Physical signs: carotid sinus tenderness, jugular venous pulse (prominent C‑wave suggests tricuspid regurgitation), peripheral pulses (weakness suggests aortic stenosis).
Bedside tests: orthostatic vitals, carotid sinus massage (if no contraindication), simple ECG. These cannot detect intermittent arrhythmias or structural heart disease beyond murmurs.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a stepwise approach, prioritising tests that change management, and adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Detects arrhythmias, conduction blocks, ischemia, new LBBB, ventricular tachycardia, significant bradycardia. New LBBB or VT warrants urgent cardiology referral.
Rule out acute coronary syndrome; values >99th percentile indicate myocardial injury.
BNP >400 pg/mL suggests heart failure or severe aortic stenosis; lower thresholds (<100 pg/mL) are less specific.
Confirm orthostatic hypotension: systolic drop ≥20 mmHg or diastolic drop ≥10 mmHg within 3 min of standing.

t.a: Carotid sinus massage (if no carotid bruit or atherosclerosis)
t.b: Positive if BP falls >50 mmHg or HR >30 bpm, indicating carotid sinus hypersensitivity.
Identify paroxysmal arrhythmias; ventricular ectopy burden >5% is a marker but not diagnostic alone.
Assess valve morphology, left ventricular outflow tract gradients, ejection fraction, and structural abnormalities.
Look for cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion, pulmonary embolism signs.
Elevated levels support further imaging; normal levels can rule out PE in low‑risk patients.

t.a: Laboratory panel (CBC, electrolytes, renal, liver, glucose)
t.b: Identify anemia, electrolyte imbalance, infection markers.

sections.p: Classify syncope using ESC/ACC risk stratification and mechanism, then stage severity to guide urgency of investigation and treatment.
b: ESC/ACC high‑risk features: known heart disease, abnormal ECG, chest pain, exertional syncope, syncope with sustained bradycardia or tachycardia, syncope with prolonged recovery, syncope with syncope‑related injury.
Low‑risk features: clear trigger, prodrome, normal exam, no cardiac history, no abnormal ECG, no sustained arrhythmia.

Mechanistic classification: cardiac (structural or rhythm), reflex (vasovagal, carotid sinus, situational), orthostatic (dehydration, autonomic failure, medication), miscellaneous (anemia, infection, PE, sickle‑cell crisis).
Severity staging: immediate danger (cardiac arrhythmia, massive PE, severe aortic stenosis), urgent (high‑risk features but stable), routine (low‑risk, stable).

sections.p: Differentiate syncope from conditions with similar presentations using specific clues and investigations.

t.b: Post‑ictal confusion, tongue biting, incontinence, prolonged recovery; EEG and video monitoring help differentiate.
Gradual onset, altered mental status, abnormal labs (electrolytes, glucose); treat underlying cause.
Low blood glucose on point‑of‑care test, neuroglycopenic symptoms; give glucose.
Sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxia; D‑dimer and CT pulmonary angiography confirm.

t.a: Orthostatic hypotension secondary to autonomic neuropathy
t.b: Gradual BP drop on standing, chronic symptoms, autonomic testing if available.
Sudden severe chest/back pain, unequal pulses, widened mediastinum on X‑ray; CT angiography needed.

sections.p: A clear ladder guides clinicians from immediate safety to definitive therapy, with explicit drug choices and red‑flag triggers for escalation.
b: 1. Immediate safety: ensure airway, breathing, circulation; protect from injury; give oxygen if hypoxic.
2. First‑line investigations: 12‑lead ECG, bedside cardiac enzymes, orthostatic BP, pulse oximetry.
3. Risk stratification: apply ESC/ACC criteria; if high‑risk, admit and monitor in telemetry.

4. Definitive treatment – cardiac syncope: urgent cardiology review, consider anti‑arrhythmic (e.g., amiodarone for ventricular tachycardia) or pacing; for severe aortic stenosis, refer for valve replacement; avoid beta‑blockers if severe stenosis without other indication.

5. Reflex/orthostatic syncope: educate on counter‑pressure maneuvers; prescribe midodrine for persistent orthostatic hypotension; avoid fludrocortisone if not available; avoid calcium channel blockers in LQT.
6. Infection‑related syncope: treat malaria, TB or sepsis with appropriate antibiotics; correct anemia with iron or transfusion; monitor haemodynamics.
7. Monitoring: continuous ECG for 24–48 h in high‑risk patients; repeat orthostatic BP after treatment; observe for recurrence or new symptoms.
8. Escalation: if recurrent syncope, new arrhythmia, or haemodynamic instability, transfer to tertiary centre for electrophysiology study or cardiac surgery.
9. Follow‑up: schedule review within 1 week for high‑risk, 4–6 weeks for low‑risk; repeat ECG and echocardiogram as indicated.
10. Avoid: non‑selective beta‑blockers in severe aortic stenosis without indication; high‑dose diuretics in orthostatic hypotension; anticholinergics in vasovagal syncope unless contraindicated.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects, interactions and management steps for drugs commonly used in syncope.
b: 1. Amiodarone – bradycardia, hypotension, pulmonary toxicity; monitor ECG, liver, thyroid, and pulmonary function; discontinue if severe.
2. Midodrine – supine hypertension, headache; advise late‑day dosing, monitor BP, adjust dose if supine BP >140/90.
3. Beta‑blockers – bradycardia, fatigue, bronchospasm; avoid in asthma, use cardioselective agents in COPD; monitor heart rate and BP.
4. Calcium channel blockers – hypotension, constipation; avoid in severe aortic stenosis; monitor BP and symptoms.
5. Antiplatelets – bleeding risk; avoid in active bleeding or severe thrombocytopenia; monitor haemoglobin and platelets.
6. Antihypertensives (diuretics, ACE‑I) – orthostatic hypotension; counsel on slow position changes, monitor orthostatic BP.
7. Herbal remedies (e.g., ginseng, St. John’s wort) – CYP450 interactions; review all supplements; advise discontinuation if interacting with anti‑arrhythmics.

sections.p: Recognise red‑flag complications early and act promptly to prevent morbidity and mortality.
b: 1. Cardiac arrhythmia – new LBBB, sustained VT, or bradycardia; immediate telemetry and cardiology referral.
2. Massive pulmonary embolism – sudden dyspnoea, chest pain, hypoxia; start anticoagulation and consider thrombolysis; transfer to ICU.
3. Aortic dissection – severe chest/abdominal pain, unequal pulses; emergent CT angiography and surgical consult.
4. Severe dehydration or hypovolaemia – hypotension, tachycardia, oliguria; give isotonic fluids, reassess BP, consider vasopressors if refractory.
5. Sepsis – fever, leukocytosis, organ dysfunction; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, source control, and supportive care.
6. Syncope with trauma – assess for head injury, spinal cord injury; CT head if altered mental status or focal deficits.
7. Persistent orthostatic hypotension despite treatment – consider autonomic testing, review medications, and refer to specialist.

sections.p: Epidemiological and clinical variables that alter presentation, investigations and therapy.
b: 1. HIV – higher prevalence of cardiomyopathy and opportunistic infections; consider HIV‑related myocarditis, TB, and drug interactions with antiretrovirals.
2. TB – can cause pericardial effusion, myocarditis, or pulmonary embolism; screen with sputum, chest X‑ray, and TB PCR.
3. Malnutrition – low albumin, anemia, electrolyte imbalance; correct before invasive procedures; avoid nephrotoxic drugs.
4. Pregnancy – avoid teratogenic drugs; beta‑blockers with caution; manage aortic stenosis with careful fluid balance; consider regional anaesthesia for valve surgery.
5. Diabetes – autonomic neuropathy increases orthostatic syncope; monitor glucose, avoid hypoglycaemic agents that lower BP.
6. Herbal remedies – e.g., ginseng, ephedra can cause tachycardia; review all supplements and advise cessation if interacting with anti‑arrhythmics.
7. Alcohol – chronic use leads to cardiomyopathy; acute intoxication causes hypotension; advise abstinence and monitor for withdrawal.
8. Renal or liver failure – alter drug clearance; avoid nephrotoxic or hepatotoxic agents; adjust dosing of anti‑arrhythmics.
9. Age extremes – elderly have higher cardiac risk, frailty; children may present with vasovagal syncope; tailor investigations accordingly.

sections.p: Tailored approaches for vulnerable populations in low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Children – focus on vasovagal and orthostatic causes; use age‑appropriate ECG interpretation; avoid beta‑blockers unless indicated.
2. Pregnancy – use non‑teratogenic drugs; prefer beta‑blockers with proven safety; monitor fetal growth; avoid aspirin for aortic stenosis.
3. Elderly – high prevalence of cardiac syncope; use low‑dose ECG monitoring; avoid polypharmacy; consider frailty scores before invasive procedures.
4. People with HIV – monitor for drug‑drug interactions with antiretrovirals; screen for opportunistic infections; adjust anti‑arrhythmic dosing.

5. Low‑resource settings – prioritize bedside tests (orthostatic BP, ECG, pulse oximetry); use point‑of‑care troponin; rely on clinical judgment when imaging unavailable; use affordable medications like amiodarone and midodrine.

facts: Syncope: sudden, brief loss of consciousness <1 min with spontaneous recovery.
Prodrome present in reflex syncope, absent in arrhythmic syncope.
Orthostatic hypotension: systolic drop ≥20 mmHg or diastolic drop ≥10 mmHg within 3 min of standing.
High‑risk ESC/ACC features: known heart disease, abnormal ECG, exertional syncope, syncope with chest pain or dyspnoea.
Low‑risk features: clear trigger, prodrome, normal exam, no cardiac history.
12‑lead ECG first investigation in any syncope patient.
New left bundle branch block, ventricular tachycardia, significant bradycardia or ischemia on ECG are red flags.
BNP >400 pg/mL is more specific for heart failure or severe aortic stenosis.
Ventricular ectopy burden >5 % is a marker of ectopy but not a direct indication of arrhythmic syncope.
Midodrine is preferred over fludrocortisone for chronic orthostatic syncope in low‑resource settings because it is inexpensive and effective.
Beta‑blockers are first‑line for long QT syndrome but are used cautiously in severe aortic stenosis.
Anticholinergic agents can be considered in vasovagal syncope but are not absolutely contraindicated.

vivas.q: Define syncope and differentiate it from seizure.
vivas.a: Syncope is a sudden, brief loss of consciousness with spontaneous recovery; seizures have post‑ictal confusion and may last longer.

vivas.q: What bedside history questions help distinguish vasovagal from cardiac syncope?
vivas.a: Ask about prodrome (light‑headedness, nausea), triggers (standing, pain), duration (<1 min), and any chest pain or palpitations. Absence of prodrome and presence of chest pain suggest cardiac cause.

vivas.q: What is the first investigation in a patient with exertional syncope?
vivas.a: A 12‑lead ECG to look for arrhythmias, conduction blocks, or ischemia.

vivas.q: Why is midodrine preferred over fludrocortisone for chronic orthostatic syncope in low‑resource settings?
vivas.a: Midodrine is inexpensive, effective, and does not require monitoring of electrolytes, unlike fludrocortisone which needs potassium checks.

vivas.q: Explain the significance of a new left bundle branch block on ECG in a syncope patient.
vivas.a: New LBBB is a red flag for structural heart disease and warrants urgent cardiology review and possible further imaging.

vivas.q: How would you manage a patient with aortic stenosis who faints while climbing stairs?
vivas.a: Urgent cardiology referral for valve assessment; consider urgent valve replacement if severe; avoid beta‑blockers unless indicated for another reason.

vivas.q: What is the role of compression stockings in orthostatic syncope?
vivas.a: They reduce venous pooling, lower orthostatic drop, and decrease fall risk.

vivas.q: Explain why beta‑blockers are used cautiously in severe aortic stenosis with syncope.
vivas.a: They can reduce heart rate and cardiac output, worsening outflow obstruction; use only if another indication exists.

vivas.q: What is sick sinus syndrome and how does it present?
vivas.a: It is sinus node dysfunction causing sinus bradycardia with pauses; presents with dizziness, syncope, and sometimes tachycardia.

vivas.q: Why is aspirin not indicated for aortic stenosis in pregnancy?
vivas.a: Aspirin does not treat the valvular lesion and may increase bleeding risk; management focuses on haemodynamic optimisation.

vivas.q: How would you manage a patient with orthostatic hypotension after diarrhoea on diuretics?
vivas.a: Stop or reduce diuretics, rehydrate, advise slow position changes, and consider compression stockings.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a prominent V wave in the jugular venous pulse?
vivas.a: It suggests tricuspid regurgitation or right‑heart failure; a prominent x‑descent is not a sign of right‑heart failure.

mcqs.q: Which ECG finding is a red flag in a syncope patient?
mcqs.e: New LBBB indicates structural heart disease.

mcqs.q: A patient with orthostatic hypotension has a systolic drop of 22 mmHg and diastolic drop of 12 mmHg within 3 min of standing. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.e: Orthostatic hypotension is defined by those drops.

mcqs.q: Which drug is preferred for chronic orthostatic syncope in low‑resource settings?
A 24‑year‑old athlete has exertional syncope and a systolic ejection murmur that increases with Valsalva. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological therapy?
mcqs.e: Beta‑blockers are first‑line for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

mistakes: Assuming any syncope is cardiac without checking for prodrome.
Misinterpreting a prominent x‑descent as right‑heart failure.
Using a ventricular ectopy burden >5 % alone to diagnose arrhythmic syncope.
Prescribing beta‑blockers in severe aortic stenosis without considering haemodynamic impact.
Ignoring orthostatic hypotension criteria (time and magnitude).
Overlooking the need for a 12‑lead ECG as first investigation.
Treating aortic stenosis in pregnancy with aspirin.
Not recognising the SAD triad as a red flag for aortic stenosis.
